title: NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of the center of Messier 4
caption: The center of the globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Hubble has broken the center of the globular cluster Messier 4 into a multitude of glowing points, each one a star, a colossal nuclear furnace. Lying 7200 light-years away, Messier 4 is relatively close to us, which makes it a prime target for study. Tens of thousands of stars belong to it.

The cluster stands out for its large population of white dwarfs, the exposed cores of old, dying stars that have shed their outer layers into space. It also hosts an unusual planet, PSR B1620-26 b, about 2.5 times the mass of Jupiter, circling a binary pair made up of a white dwarf and a pulsar, which is a kind of neutron star. The planet's age is estimated at around 13 billion years, almost three times that of the Solar System.

Since Messier 4 is bright as globular clusters go, amateur stargazers can seek it out with binoculars or a small telescope near the orange-red star Antares in Scorpius. Don't expect Hubble's detail, though. In an eyepiece it looks like a fuzzy ball of light.
scale: Messier 4 lies about 7200 light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars or a small telescope Messier 4 appears only as a fuzzy ball of light, but Hubble's sharp view resolves it into individual stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Hubble helped make the discovery of the planet PSR B1620-26 b in July 2003. This view was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters, and the cluster is also cataloged as NGC 6121.
alt: The center of a globular cluster resolved into a multitude of glowing stars.
